design_detail: Narrative clinical review. PubMed and national survey databases were searched in April 2014 and again in September 2014 with listed terms (methamphetamine, or amphetamine where appropriate; psychosis; and domain terms such as epidemiology, treatment, genetics, diagnosis, risk factors), and US and international diagnostic and clinical guidelines were reviewed (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). No eligibility criteria, record counts, selection process or quality appraisal are reported. Sections cover DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria, clinical correlates, risk factors, duration, recurrence, differential diagnosis (with the PRISM interview as a worked example) and treatment. No tables or figures; a Key points box. Read as the NIH author manuscript deposited in PMC.
can_establish: How two UCLA clinical researchers summarized, in 2014, the diagnostic criteria, risk factors, course and management of methamphetamine-associated psychosis, and which primary studies their statements rest on.
cannot_establish: Frequency, duration or recurrence rates with known precision or representativeness, because every figure is second-hand from studies chosen without stated criteria or appraisal (several key numbers trace to a single study, a general comorbidity review, or two studies from the same research group); nor the effectiveness of any treatment for psychosis outcomes, which rests on case reports, two small trials and evidence from schizophrenia.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited evidence spans US and UN drug-use surveys, 1958–1980 experimental and observational reports of amphetamine psychosis, Japanese inpatient series, Taiwanese family and comorbidity studies, an Australian study of recreational use, a Thai cohort of people first hospitalized with methamphetamine psychosis, US treatment cohorts (the authors' Methamphetamine Treatment Project), case reports, and two randomized trials.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported beyond sources, dates and search terms (Introduction, 3rd paragraph); the authors state they favoured the most recent reports and reviews.
sample.selection_effects: Selection of sources is unstated and cannot be audited. Most of the frequency, duration and recurrence figures come from hospital or treatment samples. Three cited studies are the authors' own Methamphetamine Treatment Project papers (refs 10, 11, 96) and one is a book chapter co-written by the second author (ref 87).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The review stresses that diagnosis depends on establishing the timing of use relative to symptoms (self-report timeline, collateral informants, records, urine toxicology) and notes that a urine screen does not establish the cause of a psychosis (Section 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Cited study conditions and associations: in early laboratory studies psychosis appeared 1–5 days after repeated amphetamine administration began in volunteers, and within 36 hours in people with a history of injecting amphetamine (refs 28, 29); Japanese inpatient series linked a persistent subtype lasting over 1 month with 5 or more years of use (refs 36, 37); time from first use to psychosis was 1.7 years in people who smoked versus 4.4 years in people who injected (ref 49) (Section 3; 3.1).
exposure.polysubstance: Polydrug use is listed as a risk factor for psychosis (ref 41), and other substances, including heavy alcohol use, as triggers of recurrence (3.3); not otherwise handled.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Comparisons with schizophrenia are clinical and genetic statements drawn from cited work, without study sizes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review reports that family and genetic vulnerability predicts methamphetamine psychosis, but cites no study with a measurement taken before methamphetamine use began.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable at review level. Diagnostic instruments discussed: PRISM, Diagnostic Interview Schedule, CIDI and SCID (Section 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: PRISM is described as having excellent reliability for psychotic disorder diagnoses in people with alcohol or drug use disorders (ref 67); all the structured interviews are noted to depend on self-report (Section 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Per the review's account of DSM-5 and ICD-10: transient psychotic symptoms consistent with intoxication or withdrawal are not a psychotic disorder; a methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder requires prominent hallucinations or delusions beyond the expected effects of intoxication or withdrawal; persistence for at least 1 month after the end of intoxication or acute withdrawal, onset before substance use, or non-substance-related episodes point to a primary psychotic disorder (Section 2). PRISM defines heavy use as 4 or more use episodes per week and treats psychosis persisting more than 4 weeks after cessation as primary (Section 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed by the review. Second-hand figures: up to 40% of users with transient psychotic symptoms; 26–46% of people with methamphetamine dependence with methamphetamine psychosis; 3 times the odds of psychotic symptoms with dependence than with non-dependent use; 5 times the odds during use (McKetin et al., 2013); 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence; nearly 40% diagnosed with schizophrenia within 6 years in a Thai cohort; nearly 50% of Japanese admissions with a previous episode; one 58-person randomized trial and one later randomized trial of antipsychotics. No intervals are given for any figure.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cannot be assessed: no eligibility criteria or list of considered studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinically oriented narrative summary whose numbers are all second-hand: transient symptoms in up to 40% of users (from a 2006 general comorbidity review); recovery within about a week in early studies; a minority (16–17% in two Taiwanese studies from one group) still psychotic 1–3 months into abstinence; nearly 40% diagnosed with schizophrenia within 6 years in one Thai cohort of hospitalized patients; frequent recurrence in Japanese inpatient series; two small randomized trials of antipsychotics.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents up to approximately 40% of users affected as a recent estimate; the body attributes the figure to a 2006 review of comorbidity in general (ref 17) and specifies that it refers to transient symptoms that are not a disorder (Section 2). The abstract calls psychosocial treatment of methamphetamine dependence the optimal first-line approach to reducing psychosis; the body supports this with the association between use and symptoms and with trials that reduced methamphetamine use, but cites no trial with psychosis as its outcome (2.1; 5.2). The statement that remission within 1 week of abstinence has been reported across a number of studies, so most cases may resolve without medication, carries no citation (5.1). The Key points say methamphetamine greatly increases the risk of transient and recurrent psychosis (a causal formulation from observational data) and that recommendations will involve neuroleptics, whereas the body says many cases may resolve without medication and lists risks of antipsychotics.

timeline.event: Bramness et al. narrative review proposing a stress–vulnerability model; cited here (ref 19) as the integrated continuum theory and for the anhedonia concern about D2 blockade
McKetin et al. prospective cohort: five-fold odds of psychotic symptoms during methamphetamine use with a dose-response relation, cited here as the basis for treating methamphetamine use first
Verachai et al. randomized trial of haloperidol versus quetiapine in methamphetamine-induced psychosis, cited here: both efficacious and tolerated
Wearne & Cornish narrative review of direct methamphetamine-psychosis versus schizophrenia comparisons; cites this paper among reviews of clinical profiles and recovery

replication.where_it_stands: The broad picture (common transient symptoms, a persistent minority, recurrence with renewed use, overlap with schizophrenia) is repeated across the narrative reviews read here, but they draw on overlapping and often old primary sources; the frequency and duration figures need primary-study cards before use.

funding.funder: The footnotes state that no sources of funding were used to prepare the manuscript. The PMC copy is an NIH author manuscript (NIHMSID NIHMS640645).
funding.declared_conflicts: Neither author has any conflict of interest (Footnotes, Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs, David Geffen School of Medicine. The authors cite their own Methamphetamine Treatment Project studies for treatment engagement of people with psychosis and for depression and relapse (refs 10, 11, 96).

what_would_settle_it: For frequency and duration: a prospective cohort of people who use methamphetamine recruited outside treatment, with toxicology-verified use and a temporally sensitive structured interview (such as PRISM) repeated at fixed intervals after abstinence, reporting the proportions whose symptoms resolve within 1 week, 1 month and 6 months. For management: randomized trials in methamphetamine-associated psychosis comparing antipsychotics with benzodiazepines or placebo, and psychosocial treatment with usual care, with psychosis recurrence as the primary outcome.

domains.note: A search of PubMed and national survey databases with dates (April and September 2014) and terms is reported (Introduction, last paragraph), but no eligibility criteria, record counts or selection process; the only stated principle is to incorporate the most recent reports and reviews.

The cited studies are not appraised: frequency, duration and recurrence figures are given without design or quality comments (Sections 2–3.3), and the only quality remark on a specific study is that one trial was small (N=58; 5.1). Persistence figures of 16% and 17% from two smaller studies are called 'very similar' to the nearly 40% Thai figure (3.2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 4 of 99 references are the authors' own (Methamphetamine Treatment Project papers, refs 10, 11 and 96; a chapter co-written by the second author, ref 87); ref 10 is the only source given for engagement and reduced use with Matrix Model treatment among people with psychosis (2.1).

The abstract calls psychosocial treatment of methamphetamine dependence the optimal first-line approach to reducing psychosis, while the body presents this as an argument ('it has been argued', 2.1) and cites no trial with psychosis as the outcome (5.2). The Key points say recommendations 'will involve' neuroleptics regardless of etiology, against the body's statements that evidence is insufficient for guidelines and that most cases may resolve without medication (5.1).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the course and treatment of methamphetamine psychosis
domains.note: Neither side is under-represented: competing explanations for persistent psychosis (a prolonged methamphetamine psychosis, unmasked schizophrenia, a continuum; 3.2) and both the efficacy and the risks of antipsychotics (5.1) are presented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High, because the selection of sources is unstated, the cited studies are not appraised, and the abstract and Key points state treatment conclusions that the body presents as argued or unproven. It may be cited for its account of the DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria and of the diagnostic approach (timeline of use, collateral information, urine toxicology, PRISM), and as a pointer to primary studies. Its frequency, duration and recurrence figures and its treatment recommendations may not be cited without the primary sources.

key_findings.finding: Diagnostic frame described: transient psychotic symptoms consistent with methamphetamine intoxication or withdrawal are not a psychotic disorder; a methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder needs hallucinations or delusions beyond expected effects; symptoms persisting at least 1 month after intoxication or acute withdrawal ends point to a primary psychotic disorder under DSM-5, with ICD-10 described as similar.
key_findings.locator: 2. Clinical Features of Psychosis in Methamphetamine Users, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Frequency figures cited: transient psychotic symptoms in up to 40% of people who use methamphetamine (ref 17); 26–46% of people with methamphetamine dependence have methamphetamine psychosis (ref 45); people meeting dependence criteria have 3 times the odds of psychotic symptoms of non-dependent users after controlling for history of schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders (ref 41).
key_findings.locator: Section 2, 1st paragraph; 3.1 Psychiatric and Genetic Risk Factors, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Ref 17 is a 2006 review of substance use and psychiatric comorbidity in general; ref 45, called a review of recent studies, is by its title a study of people with methamphetamine dependence in Malaysia. Check both before use.

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine use was associated with a five-fold increase in the odds of psychotic symptoms, with a dose-response relation (McKetin et al., 2013, ref 25).
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Relevance of discerning clinical features…, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In early experimental studies some but not all participants became psychotic, the amount that triggered psychosis varied, and paranoia with ideas of reference, sometimes progressing to delusions, was the most frequent symptom; psychosis appeared 1–5 days after repeated administration began (refs 28–32).
key_findings.locator: 3. Clinical Correlates of Methamphetamine Psychosis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Study conditions of experiments published 1970–1974, reported second-hand.

key_findings.finding: In Japanese studies of more than 200 inpatients, a persistent subtype lasting over 1 month was associated with 5 or more years of methamphetamine use (refs 36, 37).

Risk factors listed: schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder and schizotypal personality; methamphetamine dependence; polydrug use; affective disorders and antisocial personality disorder; family psychiatric history; sleep deprivation. Time from first use to psychosis was 1.7 years in people who smoked methamphetamine versus 4.4 years in people who injected it (ref 49), and smoking did not appear protective relative to injecting.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Psychiatric and Genetic Risk Factors, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: First-degree relatives of people with methamphetamine psychosis are reported as more than 5 times more likely to have schizophrenia (ref 47), and familial loading for schizophrenia as predicting onset and duration of methamphetamine psychosis; seven candidate genes are said to be associated with methamphetamine psychosis, overlapping with schizophrenia risk markers (ref 44).
key_findings.note: The comparison is worded as relatives versus methamphetamine users without psychosis; presumably their relatives were meant. Check ref 47.

key_findings.finding: Duration: in the earliest observational and experimental studies recovery took on average less than a week (refs 28, 30, 52, 53); 16% and 17% of methamphetamine users with psychosis were still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence in two smaller studies, in people without earlier episodes or family history of schizophrenia (refs 12, 47); in more than 1,000 people in Thailand with at least one methamphetamine-induced psychotic episode, nearly 40% had a schizophrenia diagnosis within 6 years of the first episode (ref 57).
key_findings.note: Refs 12 and 47 share their first five authors and may draw on the same sample. Wearne & Cornish (2018) report the Thai figure as 38.8% at 5 years; check ref 57.

key_findings.finding: Recurrence: in Japan's second methamphetamine epidemic nearly 50% of people admitted with methamphetamine psychosis had had it before, some readmitted more than 10 times (ref 59); reported triggers are renewed use, even of small amounts after long abstinence, other substances including heavy alcohol use, sleep deprivation and psychosocial stress; recurrent episodes resemble earlier ones and can begin within less than a week of renewed use, a propensity that can last years.

Differential diagnosis rests on the timing of use relative to symptoms, collateral informants, records and urine toxicology; a positive urine screen does not establish that methamphetamine caused the psychosis; PRISM classifies psychosis as substance-induced when it occurs only during heavy use (4 or more episodes a week) or withdrawal, and as primary when it persists more than 4 weeks after use stops.

Treatment evidence: no large randomized trials; the 2009 Cochrane review included one trial (N=58) in which olanzapine and haloperidol were both efficacious, olanzapine with better tolerability and fewer extrapyramidal symptoms (ref 79); a later randomized trial found haloperidol and quetiapine both efficacious and tolerated (ref 80); otherwise case reports. Concerns raised: D2 blockade and anhedonia possibly raising relapse risk, and a preclinical haloperidol–methamphetamine interaction; benzodiazepines may be used for agitation.
key_findings.locator: 5.1 Treatment for acute methamphetamine psychosis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that remission within 1 week of abstinence has been reported across a number of studies, so that for a large majority symptoms may resolve without medication.
key_findings.note: No citation is attached to this sentence; Section 3.2 cites refs 28, 30, 52 and 53 (1958–1980 sources) for recovery within about a week.

key_findings.finding: Little is known about antipsychotic safety and efficacy for children and adolescents with methamphetamine-induced psychosis, who are said to form a sizable subgroup of first-episode presentations (ref 88).
key_findings.note: Ref 88 is, by title, a review of atypical antipsychotics in aggressive children and adolescents, not a study of methamphetamine psychosis.

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial treatment: the Matrix Model and contingency management reduce methamphetamine use, and people with psychosis engaged in and reduced use with Matrix treatment comparably to those without (ref 10); CBT has not been formally studied for methamphetamine-induced psychotic disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says DSM-5 defines substance-induced psychosis as psychosis preceding the onset of substance use or persisting less than one month after withdrawal or intoxication; Section 2 lists onset before substance use as a sign of a primary psychotic disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 3.2 sentence is internally contradictory; the Section 2 account is the coherent one, but the DSM-5 text itself should be the source for any diagnostic statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The 16% and 17% persistence figures (refs 12, 47) are called very similar to the nearly 40% Thai figure, which they are not; the two studies share their first five authors and may not be independent; and ref 47 is cited both for familial loading predicting duration (3.1) and for persistent cases having no family history of schizophrenia (3.2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The persistence and family-history statements should be taken from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's headline of up to approximately 40% of users affected is described as recent but is cited to a 2006 general comorbidity review (ref 17); the body specifies that it refers to transient symptoms.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure should not be used as a methamphetamine prevalence estimate without the primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: Several citations do not match their claims by title: a meta-analysis of antipsychotics in schizophrenia (ref 76) is listed among case studies of antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis; a review of antipsychotics in aggressive youth (ref 88) supports the share of young people among first-episode methamphetamine psychosis; a case report of mania after sleep deprivation (ref 63) supports sleep deprivation as a trigger of recurrence.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements need primary sources before use.

reporting_issues.issue: Cross-paper: the Thai cohort (ref 57) is reported here as nearly 40% within 6 years and by Wearne & Cornish (2018) as 38.8% at 5 years; the 1.7-year latency from first use to psychosis (ref 49) is reported here for people who smoked (4.4 years for injecting) but by Wearne & Cornish as an overall average.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both figures must be checked in Kittirattanapaiboon et al. (2010) and Matsumoto et al. (2002).

reporting_issues.issue: Read from the PMC author manuscript, which may differ from the published version in CNS Drugs (2014;28:1115–1126); printed pagination is not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors are to sections of the author manuscript.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5027896 (NIH author manuscript; all sections, Key points, footnotes and references; no tables, figures or supplementary material)
